state.misconception_label: When subtracting fractions, subtracts the numerators and multiplies the denominators

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Express the following as a single fraction, writing your answer as simply as possible: \( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{t}{3} \). I got \( \frac{1-t}{3 s} \) because I treated the fractions like ordinary numbers.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: When subtracting fractions, we must find a common denominator. In this case, the common denominator is 3s. Then, we subtract the numerators. So, the correct answer is \( \frac{3-1s}{3s} \). Remember, when subtracting fractions, we keep the denominators the same.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so I need to find a common denominator first instead of just multiplying them together? So for \( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{t}{3} \), I'd convert \( \frac{1}{s} \) to \( \frac{3}{3s} \) and \( \frac{t}{3} \) to \( \frac{st}{3s} \), then subtract to get \( \frac{3-st}{3s} \)? Is that the right way to think about it?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Yes, that's correct! You found the common denominator of 3s and then subtracted the numerators. Great job on correcting your mistake. Just remember to always find a common denominator when subtracting fractions. Keep up the good work!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Thanks! So basically I need to make sure both fractions have the same bottom number before I subtract them, right? I think I've got it now, but would this work the same way if I was adding fractions instead of subtracting them?

score.justification_pass1: While the student successfully corrects their work and demonstrates improved understanding, the teacher makes a notation error in Turn 1 (writing "1s" instead of "st"), provides direct answers rather than prompting reasoning, and doesn't deeply engage with why the original misconception was problematic.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently states explicit procedures (find common denominator, subtract numerators), gives direct corrective feedback on the procedural error, and reinforces the rule, though there is a minor notational error in Turn 1 ('1s' instead of 'st').
